source_title: Delhi High Court refuses access to Race Course mosque for prayers

The Delhi High Court on Thursday declined to direct the restoration of worshippers’ access to the Race Course mosque in Lutyens’ Delhi, which faces the threat of demolition, even as the Centre assured the court that no coercive action would be taken against the structure for the time being.
Justice Anish Dayal, hearing a petition seeking protection for the mosque, noted the demolition work under way around the structure and raised concerns over the safety of worshippers. “If somebody gets injured, who is going to pay compensation?” he asked.
The Centre’s counsel, Ashish Dixit, submitted that the authorities would decide on a representation made by the Delhi Waqf Board within four weeks and that no coercive action would be taken in the meantime.
Opposing the plea to allow worshippers access to the mosque, Mr. Dixit said entry to the premises would be unsafe because of the ongoing demolition work. He added that access to a temple on the premises had also been restricted.
“Let it go. Let them decide. It is a fair submission. We can’t force them to give access for prayers,” the court told the petitioner’s counsel.
The court also directed the authorities to file a status report on the demolition activities in the area.
The petition, filed by Syed Ahmed Saud, seeks protection for the Race Course mosque, a notified Waqf property since 1977, situated within the Jaipur Polo Ground complex. The petitioner has also sought restoration of access to the mosque for offering prayers.
The Centre took over the Jaipur Polo Ground in June and the adjoining Delhi Race Club in August. The mosque stands on a land parcel taken over by the Centre for “public purpose”.
The petitioner’s counsel argued that the mosque is a Grade II protected structure and that any alteration to it required the approval of the Heritage Conservation Committee.
